trails.bestSeason: Mid-Aug to Oct (closed roughly mid-Mar-mid-Aug for peregrine falcon nesting)
trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, NPS.gov confirms this trail closes annually, typically from March through mid-August, to protect nesting peregrine falcons — always check the park's current closures page before you go, since exact dates vary by year.
trails.didYouKnow: The Precipice is one of the most exposed non-technical trails in the eastern U.S., climbing roughly 1,000 feet up sheer granite cliffs on iron rungs and ladders in well under a mile.

trails.trailTip: The open granite ridge has little shade and can be windy even on a warm day — bring layers and sun protection.
trails.didYouKnow: Cadillac Mountain is the highest point on the U.S. Atlantic coast, and from roughly early October to early March it's the first place in the country to see the sunrise.

trails.trailTip: The eastern shore crosses a short boulder field below Penobscot Mountain — wear sturdy shoes even though the trail is billed as flat.
trails.didYouKnow: Jordan Pond's water is famous for its clarity, and the trail passes directly beneath 'the Bubbles,' twin granite peaks left behind by receding glaciers.

elevationProfile.label: Loop closes near Jordan Pond House

trails.bestSeason: Late June-Oct (avoid when wet — granite gets slick)
trails.trailTip: Skip this trail in the rain — the granite ledges and iron rungs get dangerously slick, and the route isn't recommended for young children, pets, or anyone afraid of heights.
trails.didYouKnow: Despite its short length, the Beehive is one of Acadia's most thrilling hikes, gaining about 450 feet up exposed granite in under a mile via iron rungs and narrow ledges.

trails.trailTip: Time a visit near high tide for the loudest show at Thunder Hole, and stay well back from the edge on all coastal rocks — rogue waves are a real hazard.
trails.didYouKnow: Ocean Path runs almost the entire length of Park Loop Road along the shoreline, connecting Sand Beach to Otter Cliff, one of the highest headlands directly on the U.S. Atlantic coast.

trails.trailTip: The Cadillac Cliffs alternate route near the start adds a short scramble past an old sea cave — a fun detour, but skip it if the rock is wet.
trails.didYouKnow: Gorham Mountain's summit sits just 525 feet above sea level but offers one of the widest ocean panoramas in the park, taking in Sand Beach, Otter Cliff, and the open Atlantic.

trails.trailTip: Stay behind the marked barrier at Bubble Rock — the glacial erratic looks precarious but people have been injured trying to pose right beneath it.
trails.didYouKnow: Bubble Rock is a glacial erratic, a boulder carried and deposited by the ice sheet that carved Acadia's landscape thousands of years ago — geologists have traced its origin to bedrock miles away.

trails.bestSeason: Mid-Aug to Oct (closed spring-summer for peregrine falcon nesting)
trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, NPS.gov confirms this trail closes most years from around March through mid-August for peregrine falcon nesting — check current conditions before planning your hike, since exact reopening dates vary by year.
trails.didYouKnow: Jordan Cliffs gains over 1,000 feet in under a mile along its steepest cliffside section, using iron rungs bolted directly into the rock face.

elevationProfile.label: Loop closes near Jordan Pond House

trails.trailTip: Start from the far end of Sand Beach and go early to avoid crowded beach parking in summer.
trails.didYouKnow: Great Head is a granite headland shaped by the same glacial and wave action that formed Sand Beach, and it's one of the highest points directly on Acadia's coastline.

animals.whereToLook: Precipice, Jordan Cliffs, and Valley Cove cliff faces
animals.viewingTip: Use the ranger-staffed spotting scope often set up near Precipice or Jordan Pond during nesting season rather than approaching closed trails.
animals.didYouKnow: Peregrine falcons can reach speeds over 200 mph in a hunting dive, making them the fastest animal on Earth — Acadia's cliff-nesting pairs were part of the species' recovery after DDT nearly wiped it out.

animals.whereToLook: Rocky ledges and offshore islands, visible from Ocean Path or by boat tour
animals.viewingTip: Bring binoculars — seals haul out on rocks that are only exposed around low tide, and boats must keep a legal distance away.
animals.didYouKnow: Harbor seals can dive for over 20 minutes at a time, but they still need to haul out on rocks daily to rest, regulate body temperature, and avoid predators.

animals.whereToLook: Forest edges and carriage roads throughout the island
animals.viewingTip: Drive carriage roads and park roads slowly at dawn and dusk, when deer are most active near the roadside.
animals.didYouKnow: Acadia's white-tailed deer are capable swimmers and have been spotted crossing Somes Sound between the island's forested peninsulas.

animals.whereToLook: Jordan Pond, Eagle Lake, and other quiet ponds
animals.viewingTip: Keep a wide distance from shoreline nests and let chicks be — loons are easily flushed off eggs, and paddlers should give calling adults plenty of room.
animals.didYouKnow: A loon's haunting wail can carry over a mile across still water, and the species needs a long open-water runway — sometimes a quarter mile — just to take flight.

animals.whereToLook: Spruce-fir forest throughout the park, especially near conifer stands
animals.viewingTip: Follow the chattering scold call — red squirrels are territorial and loudly announce anyone passing through their patch of forest.
animals.didYouKnow: A single red squirrel can cache thousands of spruce and fir cones in a midden pile to survive Acadia's winter, sometimes reusing the same pile for generations.

animals.whereToLook: Spruce-fir forest, often resting high in tree branches
animals.viewingTip: Look up — porcupines often spend the day resting in the crooks of conifer branches rather than on the ground.
animals.didYouKnow: A porcupine carries roughly 30,000 quills, which detach easily on contact and have a barbed tip that can slowly work into skin over hours.

animals.viewingTip: Watch the water near known nest platforms — ospreys hover briefly before folding their wings into a dramatic feet-first dive for fish.
animals.didYouKnow: Ospreys have reversible outer toes and barbed foot pads that let them grip slippery fish, and they carry prey head-first in flight to reduce wind drag.

animals.whereToLook: Dense understory and thickets throughout the park
animals.viewingTip: Look for movement rather than shape in dense brush — their coat, brown in summer and white in winter, is built to disappear against the season.
animals.didYouKnow: Snowshoe hares get their name from oversized hind feet that spread their weight across snow, letting them outrun predators like lynx and fox in deep winter snowpack.

animals.whereToLook: Remote inland sections away from developed areas
animals.viewingTip: Sightings are uncommon on Mount Desert Island — if you do see one, keep a safe distance and never approach or offer food.
animals.didYouKnow: Acadia's black bear population is small and shy compared to mainland Maine, likely limited by the island's fragmented forest and proximity to development.

animals.bestSeason: Late May-mid Aug (nesting; adults depart by early Sep)
animals.whereToLook: Offshore nesting islands like Petit Manan, reached via naturalist-led boat tours departing Bar Harbor
animals.viewingTip: As of September 2026, per Bar Harbor Whale Watch Co. and Acadian Boat Tours, puffins nest on protected offshore islands with no public landing — book a naturalist-led lighthouse/puffin cruise from Bar Harbor and view the colony from the boat with binoculars rather than approaching by kayak or personal boat.
animals.didYouKnow: Puffins aren't found within Acadia's own boundaries — nearby colonies like Petit Manan Island support only a few hundred breeding pairs, so researchers there radio updates to passing tour boats in real time.
